indicator.subject: Science
indicator.content_standard: B2.3.2.1: Show understanding of the orderliness of the sun, planets and satellites in the solar system as well as the important role of the sun in the solar system
indicator.objective: Identify the sun as the main source of light and warmth on earth

skills.description: Identify the sun as the main source of both light and warmth on Earth
Explain what we use the sun's light and warmth for
Explain simply what life would be like without the sun

misconceptions: The sun only gives light; it does not give warmth.
The moon gives us more warmth than the sun.
We do not need the sun because we have electric lights and heaters.
The sun is not a star; it is just a big ball of fire.
The sun only affects plants, not people or animals.

questions.stem: What is the main source of light on Earth?
hints: It comes out in the day.
It is very bright.
questions.explanation: The sun is the main source of light on Earth.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think the moon is the main source of light.

questions.stem: What is the main source of warmth on Earth?
hints: When it is out, we feel hot.
It is in the sky during the day.
questions.explanation: The sun is the main source of warmth on Earth.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think the moon provides warmth.

questions.stem: Why do we hang wet clothes outside?
options: So the sun can dry them
So the moon can dry them
So the rain can dry them
So the wind can dry them
hints: What is in the sky outside?
It gives heat.
questions.explanation: We hang wet clothes outside so the sun's warmth can dry them.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think the wind does all the drying.

questions.stem: How does the sun help plants?
hints: Plants need light.
They turn towards the sun.
questions.explanation: The sun gives plants light and warmth, which they need to grow and make food.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think plants only need water.

questions.stem: What would happen if there was no sun?
options: It would be very dark and cold
hints: The sun gives light and warmth.
Without it, we lose both.
questions.explanation: Without the sun, the Earth would be very dark and cold.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think the moon would light up the Earth equally.

questions.stem: Which activity uses the warmth of the sun?
hints: You need heat to dry things.
The sun makes things dry.
questions.explanation: Drying fish uses the warmth of the sun to remove moisture and preserve the fish.
questions.misconception: Pupils may not connect warmth to drying.

questions.stem: Which statement is TRUE about the sun?
options: It gives both light and warmth
hints: You feel hot when it shines.
You can see because of it.
questions.explanation: The sun provides both light and warmth to the Earth.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think the sun only provides one or the other.

questions.stem: Why do we feel warm when we stand outside on a sunny day?
options: Because the sun is giving off heat
hints: The sun is out.
It provides warmth.
questions.explanation: We feel warm because the sun provides heat (warmth) to the Earth.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think the wind makes them warm.

questions.stem: If the sun stopped shining, what would happen to plants?
options: They would stop growing and die
hints: Plants need light to make food.
No light means no food.
questions.explanation: Plants need sunlight to make their food. Without the sun, they would not be able to grow and would eventually die.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think plants only need soil.

questions.stem: What is the main source of light and warmth on Earth?
hints: It is in the sky.
You see it in the day.
questions.explanation: The sun is the main source of light and warmth.

questions.stem: Name one thing you can do because of the sun's warmth.
hints: Think about wet clothes.
Think about how you feel on a sunny day.
questions.explanation: We can dry clothes or food, or keep ourselves warm thanks to the sun's warmth.
questions.misconception: Pupils may name things that use light but not warmth, like reading.

questions.stem: Why is the sun important for drying our food like gari and fish?
options: Because its warmth removes water from the food
Because it makes the food wet
Because it changes the colour of the food
Because it makes the food cold
hints: Think about what happens to water in the sun.
It evaporates.
questions.explanation: The sun's warmth causes water in the food to evaporate, which helps dry and preserve it.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think the sun adds something to the food.

questions.stem: Why can we say the sun is a star?
options: Because it is a huge ball of burning gas that gives off light and heat
Because it is small and round
Because it is in the sky
hints: Stars give off their own light.
The sun is a big ball of gas.
questions.explanation: The sun is a star because it is a massive ball of hot, glowing gas that produces its own light and heat.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think stars are only the tiny dots in the night sky.

questions.stem: If the sun stopped giving warmth, what would happen to the water in rivers and oceans?
hints: Warmth keeps water liquid.
Without heat, it gets very cold.
questions.explanation: Without the sun's warmth, the Earth would become very cold, and water would freeze into ice.
questions.misconception: Pupils may not connect the sun's warmth to the state of water.

questions.stem: Which of these is NOT a use of the sun's light?
options: Helping us see during the day
Cooking food directly without a stove
hints: Think about how food is cooked.
You need a fire or stove to cook.
questions.explanation: While the sun is hot, it cannot cook food directly without a stove or solar cooker; the others are direct uses of its light or warmth.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think the sun can cook food as fast as a fire.

questions.stem: Draw the sun and colour it. Write one word to describe what it gives us.
hints: Use yellow or orange.
What does the sun give?
questions.explanation: This tests recognising the sun and its primary outputs.

questions.stem: Explain what would happen to life on Earth if the sun suddenly disappeared.

criteria.description: States it would be very cold
States plants would die and animals/humans would struggle

hints: Think about night time.
Think about winter.
What do plants need?
questions.explanation: Without the sun, the Earth would be dark and freezing, plants would die, and life as we know it would not survive.

questions.stem: Why is the sun considered the most important object in the solar system for life on Earth?
options: Because it provides the light and warmth necessary for life
Because it is the smallest object
Because it is the only object in the sky
Because it revolves around the Earth
hints: What do living things need to survive?
Where does the energy come from?
questions.explanation: The sun is the most important object for life because it provides the light and warmth that plants, animals, and humans need to survive.
questions.misconception: Pupils may think the Earth is the centre of the solar system.

questions.stem: Write down two ways the sun helps farmers.

criteria.description: States it helps dry harvested crops/food (warmth)

hints: What do plants need?
What happens to maize after harvesting?
questions.explanation: The sun helps farmers by providing light for crops to grow and warmth to dry harvested produce.

questions.stem: Tell your teacher why the sun is important for both light and warmth.

criteria.description: States we need light to see
States we need warmth to stay warm/dry things

hints: What happens at night?
What happens when it is cold?
questions.explanation: The sun gives us light to see during the day and warmth to keep us from freezing and to dry our food and clothes.
